title: The August Reset: Why Debtor Days Creep Back Up Once the EOFY Push Fades
linkedin:
Every owner-led business tightens its collections process before 30 June. Almost none of them keep doing it in August.

Here is the pattern we see every winter. In the run up to EOFY, someone is checking the receivables balance daily, chasing overdue accounts, following up faster than usual, because everyone understands that the debtors number on 30 June becomes the opening cash position for the new year.

Then July starts. The deadline that drove all that intensity is gone, and so is the reason to keep it up. Attention moves back to the work in front of the business.

Take a business that works its ledger hard enough to bring Days Sales Outstanding down to 35 days by 30 June. By August, with no one deciding to ease off, that same number can sit back at 45 or 50 days without a single conscious choice being made.

The cost lands at an awkward time. Supplier payments and quarterly obligations do not slow down just because collections have, which means a business can end up quietly financing an extra month of receivables right when its own cash flow discipline should be resetting for the year ahead, not unwinding.

The fix is not chasing harder in June. It is building a collections rhythm, weekly ledger reviews, a follow up sequence that triggers on terms rather than on memory, that holds through the quiet months without needing a deadline to enforce it.

A note for business owners on the east coast this month. If your team pushed hard on overdue invoices before 30 June, it is worth checking the debtors ledger again now, because that same discipline tends to fade once the year end deadline passes.

The pattern we see often is straightforward. The intensity around collections in June is usually driven by a fixed date, not an ongoing system. Once that date passes, invoicing returns to its normal rhythm, follow up calls lose their urgency, and the ledger that looked tight in June can quietly drift back out over July and August without anyone making a conscious decision to let it happen.

The timing is awkward too. Supplier payments and quarterly obligations do not slow down just because collections have, so a business can end up financing extra weeks of receivables right when cash discipline for the new financial year should be settling in, not loosening.

A weekly review of the ledger, rather than a monthly one, and a follow up process that triggers automatically once an invoice passes terms, are usually enough to hold the line without needing another EOFY scramble to fix it next year.
